extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers, students and scholars of race, history, and sociology
extracted.subtask_description: A historical-sociological analysis (early 20th century) of the condition, progress, and proposed solutions to 'the Negro problem' worldwide, with statistics, classifications of policy approaches, and commentary on colonialism, economics, and rising racial consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and economic indicators of Negro progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures of the Negro population's material condition and progress over fifty years (numbers in population, acreage owned, farms, property values, occupations, homes, schoolchildren).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists census-style statistics: population growth (e.g., from ~5 million in 1863 to over 10 million in 1913 in the U.S.), acres of land owned rising from a few million after the war to nearly 20,000,000 by 1910, increases in number and value of farms (120,738 farms in 1890 to 218,972 in 1910; farm values from $179,796,639 in 1900 to $440,992,439 in 1910), counts of breadwinners, occupational breakdowns (farm owners, tenants, miners, building trades, railway employees, professional service including teachers/clergymen/physicians), 2,175,000 Negro homes, and 1,620,000 children in school. These figures are used as empirical criteria for judging economic advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property ownership and land-holding as progress metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent and value of land, farms, homes, and total property held by Negroes as a measure of uplift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes acres owned (estimates across decades), increases in the number of farms (e.g., 120,738 in 1890 to 218,972 in 1910), home ownership (about 500,000 homes in 1910), and total property value (American Economic Association estimate of $300,000,000 in 1900, projected to $800,000,000). These data serve to evaluate economic independence and material progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational distribution and labor status
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of the occupational breakdown (laborers, servants, tenant farmers, skilled workers, owners/managers, professional classes) as an indicator of social and economic mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides counts for various fields (e.g., 218,972 farm owners; 319,346 cash tenants; 134,102 railway employees; 29,750 teachers; 17,495 clergymen; 4,546 physicians/dentists/nurses). The movement from penniless field hands toward skilled employment and ownership is used to assess advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional development (churches, schools, societies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence, scale, and resources of Negro-led institutions—churches, schools and colleges, secret and beneficial societies, hospitals, orphanages, cemeteries, and banks—as measures of communal organization and self-help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nearly 40,000 churches with edifices worth at least $75,000,000 controlling ~4,000,000 members; 200 private Negro schools/colleges largely managed and supported by Negroes; $45,000,000 raised over 40 years by Negro schools; $7,500,000 raised annually for churches; five million dollars a year raised by secret societies holding $6,000,000 in real estate; over 22,000 small retail businesses and 40 banks. The existence and financial strength of these institutions are cited as evidence of internal organization and uplift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literacy and cultural expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Rates of literacy and the growth of cultural output (papers, periodicals, poetry, literature, music, painting) as indicators of spiritual and intellectual advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts nine-tenths illiteracy in 1860 with over two-thirds literacy by the present time; notes 300 papers and periodicals and recognition of Negro contributions to the arts. These cultural markers are treated as measures of self-expression and maturity of the race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political participation and civic recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which Negroes hold public office, vote, and serve in national forces as measures of their recognition within government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited indicators include holding 7,500 offices in the executive national service, furnishing four regiments in the army and many sailors, nearly 20,000 state and municipal offices, and furnishing 500,000 votes which influence the Union. Even with disfranchisement, such metrics indicate political integration and responsibility-sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: First suggested solution: uplift along European/American lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy approach that assumes Negro uplift should follow the same path as European and American whites—education, partial enfranchisement, elementary rights of wage earners and property holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the 'first' solution historically suggested: giving partial enfranchisement and education, recognizing independence of Liberia and Haiti, and expecting the working class' uplift to mirror that of whites. The text implies this was the initial, optimistic policy response after emancipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second suggested solution: virtual enslavement/forced labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy of maintaining coerced labor for extractive industries—de facto or 'forced' labor defended as necessary for implanting modern industry in 'barbarous' lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by rubber and ivory collection in the Belgian Congo, cocoa in Angola, and diamond mining in South Africa. The author notes its close likeness to slavery, partial modification over time, and the economic motives behind its defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third suggested solution: land monopoly and restricted education to produce docile labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy of using land monopoly, taxation, and minimal education to create a docile industrial class working for low wages and unable to organize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include peonage in parts of the United States and labor systems in African colonies, and the West Indian islands where land and capital management reduced black peasantry to straits despite abundant resources. The text frames this as an indirect method to secure cheap labor without overt forced slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth suggested solution: native structures maintained under European control (indirect rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy to preserve outward native structures—kings, native courts, family and religion—while subjecting them to the veto and command of a European magistracy backed by native armies with European officers, thereby limiting education, political development, and economic autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the then-popular approach: on its face it offers abolition of slave trade and suppression of warfare and encourages peaceful industry, but in practice serves economic motives—using land and people for European benefit, limiting education and modern religion, and protecting white mercantile exploitation. The text highlights both apparent advantages and underlying exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation and separation as subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Segregation framed as a variant of the 'fourth' solution: ostensibly separation of races but in practice subordination and enforced distance from civilization in dwelling, education, and public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author applies this to attempts at segregation of Negroes and mulattoes in the United States and West Indies, noting its pretense of separation while functioning to subordinate colored people under white tutelage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic significance of Negro labor and exports
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the current and potential economic value of Negro labor and exports (e.g., African and West Indies export figures) as a factor in global economic and political strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites figures: Black Africa exports nearly $200 million annually, the black West Indies nearly $100 million, plus labor value across many regions. These economic stakes are used to explain motives behind colonial policies and the global importance of the 'Negro problem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pan-African unity and solidarity as a future metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that future Pan-African movement will not be narrow racial propaganda but will unify working classes, colored races, and broader humanity; the degree of such unity is posited as a criterion of future progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes emerging signs: intellectual centers in the U.S. and West Indies, growing interest in brotherhood of Negro blood, and the view that modern white laborers hold the key to black liberation. The shape and extent of solidarity among colored races and with white labor are treated as indicators of progress toward global justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of self-realization and leadership within the race
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of Negro self-leadership, voices, ideals, and asserting rights as a qualitative measure of advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual markers: movement from being led and defended by others to gaining own leaders and ideals, increased protest and manly self-assertion, and engagement with wider ideals such as emancipation of women, universal peace, democratic government, and human brotherhood.
